title: Figma vs Sketch: A Deep Dive for Design Teams
description: A detailed comparison of Figma and Sketch covering collaboration, prototyping, design systems, developer handoff, and platform strategy — with a clear recommendation for which teams should choose which tool.
body:
Figma and Sketch have defined the UI design tool category for over a decade, but their trajectories have diverged significantly. Figma has evolved from a browser-based design tool into a collaborative design platform that covers whiteboarding, prototyping, design system management, and developer handoff. Sketch has remained a Mac-native desktop application focused on vector editing and interface design, with cloud collaboration added as a secondary capability.

This comparison examines the practical differences between these tools across the dimensions that matter most to design teams: collaboration, prototyping, design systems, developer handoff, and long-term platform viability.

## Collaboration Model

Figma's collaboration is built on real-time multiplayer editing. Multiple designers work on the same file simultaneously, with visible cursors, selection indicators, and live updates. This collaboration model extends to prototyping, where team members can test interactive flows together during design reviews. Figma's commenting system supports inline comments on any element, frame, or prototype step, and comments resolve into actionable design changes.

Sketch's collaboration requires Sketch for Teams or Sketch Cloud. Multiple designers can work on files within the same project, but simultaneous editing of the same file is limited. Sketch Cloud provides a web viewer for review and commenting, but the collaboration experience is secondary to the design editing experience. For small teams where designers work on distinct areas of the product, Sketch's collaboration model is adequate. For larger teams that need real-time co-editing, Figma provides a fundamentally different experience.

The collaboration gap between Figma and Sketch is the most significant differentiator for team-based workflows. Figma's multiplayer editing eliminates the file-based workflow that Sketch requires, where designers work on separate files and merge changes through version control.

## Prototyping Capabilities

Figma's prototyping supports click-through flows, smart animate transitions, conditional logic, state management, and overflow behavior. The interaction panel defines triggers (tap, hover, drag), actions (navigate to, open overlay, swap), and animations (dissolve, move, slide) without leaving the design canvas. Figma's variable-based prototyping allows designers to define state — toggling visibility, changing text, or switching themes — and wire complex multi-step flows.

Sketch's prototyping connects artboards with hotspot links and defines transition animations. The interaction model is adequate for linear user flows — onboarding sequences, checkout funnels, or navigation paths — but lacks the conditional logic and state management that Figma provides. Teams using Sketch for prototyping often supplement it with Principle, ProtoPie, or Figma itself for complex interactions.

The prototyping gap is significant for product teams that need to test complex user flows. Figma's prototyping capabilities reduce the need for dedicated prototyping tools, whereas Sketch's limitations require supplementary tools for anything beyond basic click-throughs.

## Design System Management

Figma's design system management uses component libraries with variants, auto-layout, component properties, and nested instances. Libraries publish across files, enabling design teams to consume shared components while maintaining local overrides. Figma's library analytics show which components are most used and which are underutilized, providing data-driven insight into design system adoption.

Sketch's design system management uses shared libraries with symbols, nested symbols, and shared styles. Libraries sync through Sketch Cloud, and team members consume components from shared libraries. Sketch's library management is mature and well-tested, with a decade of refinement in its symbol and style systems.

Both tools provide capable design system management, but Figma's component properties system — boolean toggles, text properties, instance swap, and variant properties — provides more granular control over component customization than Sketch's symbol override system.

## Developer Handoff

Figma's Dev Mode provides inspect panels showing CSS, iOS, and Android code snippets for any selected element. Developers view component properties, design tokens, spacing values, and asset export specifications without leaving Figma. The integration with Figma's branching system means developers always reference the latest approved design state.

Sketch's developer handoff uses its inspection panel and integration with third-party tools like Zeplin. The native inspect panel shows dimensions, colors, fonts, and spacing, but lacks the component-level detail and design token integration that Figma's Dev Mode provides. Teams using Sketch for handoff typically pair it with Zeplin or Abstract for structured handoff workflows.

Figma's integrated handoff reduces friction between design and development, while Sketch's reliance on third-party tools adds integration overhead.

## Platform Strategy and Long-Term Viability

Figma's platform strategy is consolidation — building an ecosystem that covers the entire design workflow from brainstorming through production. The 2025 Figma Config announcements focused on AI features, design-to-code generation, and expanded platform capabilities. Figma's browser-based architecture enables cross-platform collaboration without platform constraints.

Sketch's platform strategy is refinement — continuing to improve its Mac-native design tool while adding cloud features for collaboration. Sketch's desktop application provides performance and offline capabilities that browser-based tools cannot match, but its Mac-only constraint limits its addressable market as teams increasingly include Windows and Linux users.

The platform strategy divergence creates different risk profiles. Figma risks over-extension as it expands into adjacent categories. Sketch risks irrelevance as the design tool market consolidates around cross-platform collaborative platforms.

## Recommendation

For teams with more than three designers that need real-time collaboration, Figma provides the most productive workflow. For Mac-native teams with fewer than five designers that prioritize design tool performance over collaboration features, Sketch provides a capable alternative at a lower subscription cost. For teams that need to support designers on Windows or Linux, Figma is the only viable option of the two.

The transition cost from Sketch to Figma is non-trivial — design files require conversion, workflows need adjustment, and team members need training. Teams considering a migration should budget for this transition cost and evaluate whether the collaboration benefits justify the migration investment.

Both tools serve the core design workflow effectively. The choice between them depends on team size, platform requirements, and the value placed on real-time collaboration versus native application performance.
